title: Thyme
subtitle: The kitchen herb with the chest: infusions, syrups, and steam for coughs and colds
excerpt: Thyme is the most useful respiratory herb in the kitchen garden. The fresh or dried leaves are prepared as a steam inhalation for blocked sinuses, a short infusion for a cough, or simmered into a syrup with honey. A bunch of fresh thyme or a sealed jar of dried leaf keeps the herb available for any winter chest cold.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), thyme entry, Botanical.com transcription. Nicholas Culpeper, Complete Herbal (1653), thyme entry, public domain. glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or preparation traditionally used to loosen mucus from the respiratory tract and make coughing more productive.

A herb containing constituents, typically volatile oils, with demonstrated antimicrobial properties in laboratory settings. Not a medical claim: traditional use is in supportive preparations, not as antibiotic treatment.

content.text: Thyme in the home medicine cupboard, fresh or dried leaves for a steam, a hot infusion, or a honey syrup at the first signs of a chest cold or cough. The most versatile respiratory herb in an ordinary kitchen, long prepared as a warming remedy for coughs, congestion, and the uncomfortable chesty phase of a cold. A jar of dried thyme keeps 12 months. fresh thyme from the garden is ready all year in mild climates.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Thymus vulgaris L., family Lamiaceae. A small aromatic subshrub, 15 to 30 cm, with tiny grey-green leaves and pale lilac flowers from late spring into summer. Native to the western Mediterranean, grown in kitchen gardens across temperate Europe. The aerial parts, leaves and small stems, are used fresh or dried. Harvest before or at flowering, when the volatile oil content is highest. A related species, Thymus zygis, is used similarly and is the source of much commercial thyme oil.
Thyme leaf contains thymol and carvacrol as its key active compounds. These give thyme its
character. The leaf oil also acts as an
, loosening mucus in the airways. Current guidance supports use for mild chest infections.

The 17th-century herbalist Culpeper recommended thyme boiled in water for coughs and shortness of breath. The 20th-century herbalist Grieve records its use in whooping cough syrups, as a tea for sore throats, and as a steam for head colds. The Eclectic tradition used thyme for bronchitis and spasmodic cough. Modern herbal practice approves thyme for upper respiratory mucus and bronchitis. Current herbal guidance supports traditional use for coughs with mucus and mild throat irritation.
Hot infusion: 1 to 2 teaspoons of fresh thyme (or 1 teaspoon of dried) per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 8 to 10 minutes. Three cups a day while symptoms persist, up to 7 days.

Honey syrup: a handful of fresh thyme simmered in 300 ml of water for 15 minutes, strained, cooled, and stirred into equal volume of honey. 1 tablespoon up to three times a day. Keeps refrigerated for three weeks.

Steam inhalation: a handful of dried thyme added to a bowl of just-boiled water. Lean over the bowl with a towel draped over head and bowl, and breathe through the nose for 5 to 10 minutes. Not for children under seven.
Pregnancy: culinary quantities are safe. Avoid regular medicinal doses in pregnancy, especially in the first three months. Consult a herbalist or midwife.

When to see a doctor: a cough producing green, yellow, or blood-tinged sputum warrants medical attention. A cough with high fever, chest pain, breathlessness at rest, or any cough lasting beyond three weeks should be assessed by a doctor rather than managed at home.
